reasoning: Classic Go concurrency bug. The global cache variable is a plain map with no synchronization, but the default HTTP server dispatches each request in a separate goroutine. Concurrent reads and writes to a Go map without a mutex cause a runtime panic. The issue provides exact error output, specific reproduction steps, and the code confirms the root cause. No open PRs, no duplicates, no prerequisites.

triage_summary.title: Cache server panics under concurrency due to unsynchronized map access
triage_summary.problem: The global cache map in main.go is a plain Go map accessed concurrently by HTTP handlers without any synchronization, causing fatal error: concurrent map read and map write panics under load.
triage_summary.root_cause_hypothesis: Go built-in maps are not safe for concurrent use. The default HTTP handler spawns a new goroutine per request, so getHandler and setHandler race on the shared cache map. The Go runtime detects this and panics.
reproduction_steps: Send concurrent requests with hey -n 1000 -c 50 against the server /set endpoint on port 8080
Server panics within seconds with fatal error: concurrent map read and map write
triage_summary.impact: Server crashes completely under any concurrent load, making it unusable in production or any multi-client scenario.
triage_summary.recommended_fix: Protect the cache map with a sync.RWMutex - use RLock/RUnlock in getHandler and Lock/Unlock in setHandler. Also protect the delete(cache, key) call in getHandler by upgrading to a write lock when expiry eviction occurs.
triage_summary.proposed_test_case: Write a concurrency test that exercises the race condition: launch the server in a test goroutine, spawn N goroutines (e.g., 100) that each call /set with unique keys and /get concurrently, use go test -race to verify no data races are detected, and assert the server does not panic and all requests return valid HTTP status codes.
